title: Queue, plus stack & queue problems
overview: Module 14 introduces the queue (First-In-First-Out) — built on a singly linked list, a doubly linked list and the STL `list`, then the STL `queue` itself. The rest of the folder is practice: stack/queue exercises from the practice day, classic LeetCode and Code360 problems (valid parentheses, min stack, queue from stacks and the reverse), and a review of Module 11's linked list problems. Files that are only a judge solution run here with a small test harness.

concepts.explain: A queue is a line at a counter: new people join at the back, service happens at the front. The first value pushed is the first popped.
`push` (join the back), `pop` (leave the front), `front`, `back`, `size`, `empty` — all O(1).
With a singly linked list, remove at the **head** (O(1)) and add at the **tail** (O(1) with a `tail` pointer). Removing at the tail would need the previous node.
Pouring values through a stack reverses them; through a queue they stay in order. Many problems (reverse a queue, reverse first K) are just this idea.
When the latest unmatched item must be handled first — brackets, backspaces, adjacent duplicates — a stack is the natural tool.
A second stack that only stores 'new minimum so far' values gives `getMin` in O(1). Push on `<=` so duplicates of the minimum are counted.
A stack can be made from a queue and a queue from a stack by moving elements between helper containers. One operation becomes O(n), the rest stay O(1).
LeetCode and Code360 files contain only a class or function; the judge supplies `main`, includes and `ListNode`/`Node`. The page shows a small test driver that does that job so the code can run.

files.title: STL `queue<int>`
files.what: Uses the built-in `queue<int>`: push `n` values, show front, back and size, then pop everything in arrival order.
steps: Read `n` and `push` each value (it joins at the back).
Print `q.front()`, `q.back()` and `q.size()` on one line.
`while(!q.empty())`: print `q.front()` and `q.pop()` it.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input_note: `n`, then `n` values.
files.output_note: `1 4 4` = front, back, size. Then `1 2 3 4` one per line — the same order as the input (FIFO).
files.watch_out: Like `stack::pop`, `queue::pop` returns nothing, and calling `front()`/`pop()` on an empty queue is undefined — check `empty()` first.

check.q: What is the difference between `q.front()` and `q.back()`?
check.a: `front()` is the oldest value (next to leave); `back()` is the newest (last pushed).

files.title: Queue on a singly linked list (does not compile)
files.what: The Module 13 queue finished: push at `tail`, pop at `head`, plus a `main` that prints front, back, size and then empties the queue.
steps: `push`: new node after `tail`; the first node becomes both `head` and `tail`.
`pop`: delete `head`, move `head` forward, and reset `tail` if the queue became empty.
`front` → `head->val`, `back` → `tail->val`, `empty` → `head == NULL`.
`main` reads values, prints `front back size`, then pops and prints each value.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input_note: `n`, then `n` values.
files.output_note: No output: the file fails to compile. The working copy `queue_input_output_singly_list.cpp` shows what it would print.
files.watch_out: Compile error: the class declares both `int size = 0;` and `int size()`. Fix: rename the counter to `sz` — exactly what `queue_input_output_singly_list.cpp` does.

check.q: Why is the head the front of the queue, not the tail?
check.a: In a singly linked list you can delete the head in O(1), but deleting the tail needs the node before it (O(n)). So remove at the head and add at the tail.

files.title: Queue on a singly linked list (working)
files.what: Same singly linked queue, with the counter renamed to `sz`, so it compiles and runs.
steps: `push` increments `sz` and links the node after `tail`.
`pop` decrements `sz`, removes `head`, and clears `tail` when empty.
`size()` returns `sz`.
`main` prints `front back size` and then drains the queue.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input_note: `n`, then `n` values.
files.output_note: `5 7 3` (front 5, back 7, size 3), then `5 6 7` one per line.

check.q: What single change makes this file compile when the previous one doesn't?
check.a: The counter is named `sz` instead of `size`, so it no longer clashes with the `size()` method.

files.title: Queue on a doubly linked list (does not compile)
files.what: A queue on `Node`s with `next` and `prev`: push after `tail`, pop at `head` and clear the new head's `prev`.
steps: `push` links the node after `tail` and sets `newNode->prev = tail`.
`pop` moves `head` forward and deletes the old head.
If the queue is now empty, `tail = NULL`; otherwise `head->prev = NULL` so no pointer refers to freed memory.
`main` is the same as the singly linked version.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input_note: `n`, then `n` values.
files.output_note: No output: compile error. When fixed it prints `10 40 4` and then `10 20 30 40`.
files.watch_out: Compile error: the class declares both `int size = 0;` and `int size()`. Fix: rename the counter to `sz` — exactly what `queue_input_output_singly_list.cpp` does.

check.q: Does a queue need the `prev` pointer?
check.a: No. A queue only removes at the head and adds at the tail, both O(1) with a singly linked list; `prev` is extra memory.

files.title: Queue on the STL list
files.what: `myQueue` wraps a `list<int>`: `push_back` to join, `pop_front` to leave.
steps: `push` → `l.push_back`; `pop` → `l.pop_front`.
`front`/`back`/`size`/`empty` forward to the list.
`main` prints `front back size`, then drains the queue.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input_note: `n`, then `n` values.
files.output_note: `10 40 4`, then `10 20 30 40` one per line.

check.q: Which `list` call removes the front of the queue?
check.a: `pop_front()`.

files.title: Practice 1 · Are two stacks the same? (no STL)
files.what: Builds two stacks with the hand-made doubly linked `myStack` and compares them top to top.
steps: Read `n` values into `s1` and `m` values into `s2`.
Different sizes → print `NO` immediately.
Otherwise pop both together, comparing `top()` each time; any mismatch sets `flag = false`.
Print `YES` if every pair matched.
files.input_note: `n`, `n` values, `m`, `m` values.
files.output_note: `YES` — both stacks hold `10 20 30 40 50` in the same order.

check.q: Two stacks built from `1 2 3` and `3 2 1` — same or not?
check.a: Not the same: the tops are `3` and `1`, so the first comparison fails and the answer is `NO`.

files.title: Practice 2 · Stack vs queue in removal order
files.what: Checks whether a stack and a queue give the same values in the order they are removed.
steps: Push `n` values into `st` and `m` values into `q`.
`compareStackQueue` gets copies (passed by value) so the originals stay intact.
Different sizes → `false`.
Otherwise compare `st.top()` with `q.front()` and pop both, until empty.
files.input_note: `n` and the stack values, then `m` and the queue values.
files.output_note: `YES` — the stack gives `50 40 30 20 10` (LIFO) and the queue was filled as `50 40 30 20 10` (FIFO), so both remove the same sequence.

check.q: If both are filled with `10 20 30`, what is printed and why?
check.a: `NO` — the stack removes `30` first but the queue removes `10` first.

files.title: Practice 3 · Copy a stack to print in insertion order (bug)
files.what: Meant to print the stack values in the order they were pushed. It copies the stack twice, which puts the order back the way it was.
steps: Push the values into `st1` (top is the last value).
Pop everything into `st2` — now the first value is on top.
Pop everything again into `st3` — the order flips back, the last value is on top again.
Print `st3` by popping.
files.input_note: `n`, then `n` values.
files.output_note: Prints `50 40 30 20 10`, but the task expects `10 20 30 40 50`. Each copy reverses the order, so two copies cancel out.
files.watch_out: Bug: one copy too many. Print from `st2` (skip `st3`) and the output becomes `10 20 30 40 50`.

check.q: How many times do you need to move a stack into another stack to reverse its order?
check.a: Once. An even number of moves gives the original order back.

files.title: Practice 4 · Copy a queue in reverse order
files.what: Reverses a queue into a new queue by passing the values through a stack.
steps: Push `n` values into `q`.
Move everything from `q` into `st` — the last value ends on top.
Move everything from `st` into `q2` — the last value goes first.
Print `q2` from front to back.
files.input_note: `n`, then `n` values.
files.output_note: `50 40 30 20 10` — the input order reversed.

check.q: Why is a stack the right helper here?
check.a: A stack outputs values in the reverse of their input order, which is exactly the reversal we need.

files.title: Implement stack using queues
files.what: A stack built on one `queue<int>`. `push` just joins the queue; `pop` moves every value except the last into a helper queue and returns that last one.
steps: `push(x)` → `q.push(x)`.
`pop`: take values from `q` one by one; the last one taken (when `q` becomes empty) is the answer and is not copied.
All earlier values go into `q2`; then `q = q2`.
`top` is simply `q.back()` — the newest value.
Harness: reads commands (`push x`, `pop`, `top`, `empty`) and prints each result.
files.input:
8
push 1
push 2
push 3
top
pop
top
pop
empty
files.input_note: First the number of commands, then one command per line.
files.output_note: After pushing 1, 2, 3: `top -> 3`, `pop -> 3`, then `top -> 2`, `pop -> 2`, and the stack is not empty (1 is left) — LIFO behaviour.

check.q: Why can `top()` use `q.back()` directly?
check.a: The newest value is always at the back of the queue, and the newest value is the top of a stack.

files.title: Implement queue using stacks
files.what: A queue built on one `stack<int>`. To reach the oldest value (at the bottom) it pours the stack into a helper stack and back.
steps: `push(x)` → `st.push(x)`.
`pop`: pop values off `st` into `st2` until the last one (the bottom = oldest) is taken; that is the answer.
Pour `st2` back into `st` to restore the order.
`peek`: pour everything into `st3` (the last `val` seen is the bottom), then pour back.
Harness: reads `push x` / `pop` / `peek` / `empty` commands.
files.input:
8
push 1
push 2
push 3
peek
pop
pop
peek
empty
files.input_note: First the number of commands, then one command per line.
files.output_note: After pushing 1, 2, 3: `peek -> 1`, `pop -> 1`, `pop -> 2`, `peek -> 3` — values leave oldest first (FIFO).
files.watch_out: This file already has its includes and `using namespace std`, so the harness only adds a `main`.

check.q: What is the classic way to make `pop` amortised O(1) here?
check.a: Use two stacks: `in` for pushes and `out` for pops; only when `out` is empty, pour all of `in` into it.

files.title: Implement queue using stacks (practice copy)
files.what: Identical logic to the original, only re-indented.
steps: Same `pop`/`peek` pouring between stacks.
files.input:
8
push 1
push 2
push 3
peek
pop
pop
peek
empty
files.input_note: Number of commands, then one command per line.
files.output_note: Same commands as the original and the same results: `peek -> 1`, `pop -> 1`, `pop -> 2`, `peek -> 3`.

check.q: In `pop`, why does the loop `break` before pushing the last value into `st2`?
check.a: That last value is the oldest one — the one we remove — so it must not be put back.

files.title: Valid parentheses
files.what: Uses a stack of open brackets. Each closing bracket must match the most recent unmatched opening bracket.
steps: Opening bracket `(`, `{`, `[` → push it.
Closing bracket with an empty stack → `false` (nothing to close).
Closing bracket that matches `st.top()` → pop; otherwise → `false`.
At the end the string is valid only if the stack is empty (no bracket left open).
Harness: reads several strings and prints `true`/`false` for each.
files.input_note: Number of strings, then one bracket string per line.
files.output_note: `()[]{}` and `{[]}` are `true`. `(]` and `([)]` fail on a mismatched close; `((` fails because two brackets stay open.

check.q: Why is `([)]` invalid even though the counts match?
check.a: When `)` arrives, the top of the stack is `[`, not `(` — brackets must close in reverse order of opening.

files.title: Backspace string compare
files.what: `#` means backspace. Each string is typed into a stack (pop on `#`), then the two stacks are compared.
steps: For each char of `s`: `#` pops (if not empty), anything else is pushed.
Do the same for `t` into `st2`.
`st == st2` compares the two stacks element by element.
Harness: reads pairs of strings and prints the result.
files.complexity: Time O(n + m) · Space O(n + m)
files.input:
3
ab#c ad#c
ab## c#d#
a#c b
files.input_note: Number of pairs, then `s t` on each line (the strings contain no spaces).
files.output_note: `ab#c` and `ad#c` both become `ac` → `true`. `ab##` and `c#d#` both become empty → `true`. `a#c` is `c` and `b` is `b` → `false`.

check.q: What does `a##b` become?
check.a: `b` — the second `#` hits an empty stack and is ignored.

files.title: Remove all adjacent duplicates in a string

problem.name: LeetCode 1047 - Remove All Adjacent Duplicates In String

files.what: Pushes characters on a stack; when the new character equals the top, both cancel out (pop). What remains, read bottom to top, is the answer.
steps: For each char `c`: if the stack is not empty and `st.top() == c`, pop; else push.
Pop everything into `newS` — this gives the characters in reverse.
`reverse(newS)` restores the right order.
Harness: prints the result in quotes so an empty answer is visible.
files.input_note: Number of strings, then one string per line.
files.output_note: `abbaca` → `bb` cancels, then `aa` cancels → `"ca"`. `abba` cancels completely → `""`.

check.q: Why is the string reversed at the end?
check.a: Popping a stack gives the characters from last to first.

files.title: Min stack
files.what: Keeps a second stack `min_st` whose top is always the current minimum, so `getMin` is O(1).
steps: `push(val)`: push to `st`; also push to `min_st` if it is empty or `val <= min_st.top()`.
`pop()`: if the value leaving equals `min_st.top()`, pop `min_st` too; then pop `st`.
`top()` → `st.top()`; `getMin()` → `min_st.top()`.
Harness: runs LeetCode's example commands, plus one more push.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input:
9
push -2
push 0
push -3
getMin
pop
top
getMin
push -2
getMin
files.input_note: Number of commands, then one command per line.
files.output_note: This is LeetCode's example: after pushing -2, 0, -3, `getMin -> -3`; after one pop, `top -> 0` and `getMin -> -2`, as expected.

check.q: Why push to `min_st` when `val` is **equal** to the current minimum (`>=`, not `>`)?
check.a: With duplicates of the minimum, popping one copy would otherwise remove the minimum from `min_st` while another copy is still in `st`.

files.title: Min stack (Code360 version)
files.what: Same two-stack idea as LeetCode's Min Stack, but `pop`, `top` and `getMin` return `-1` when the stack is empty, and `pop` returns the removed value.
steps: `push`: same rule — push to `min_st` if empty or `num <= min_st.top()`.
`pop`: return `-1` if empty; otherwise pop `min_st` when the tops match, then pop and return the value.
`top`/`getMin` return `-1` on an empty stack.
Harness: pushes 5, 3, 3, 7 and pops step by step.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input:
10
push 5
push 3
push 3
push 7
getMin
pop
pop
getMin
pop
getMin
files.input_note: Number of commands, then one command per line.
files.output_note: The minimum stays `3` after popping one `3` (the duplicate is still there), and becomes `5` only after the second `3` is popped.

check.q: After pushing 5, 3, 3, what does `min_st` contain (bottom to top)?
check.a: `5 3 3` — each `3` is `<=` the current minimum, so both are stored.

files.title: Kevin's stack problem (reverse a string)
files.what: Reverses a string by pushing every character on a stack and popping them into the result.
steps: Push each character of `s`.
Pop until empty, appending each top to `result`.
Return `result` — the characters in reverse.
Harness: reads several words and prints each reversed.
files.input_note: Number of words, then one word per line.
files.output_note: `abc` → `cba`, `stack` → `kcats`.
files.watch_out: The judge adds `using namespace std;` for you; that is why the file uses `string` and `stack` without `std::`.

check.q: What is a simpler STL way to do the same thing?
check.a: `reverse(s.begin(), s.end())` — the stack version is for practising LIFO.

files.title: Stack with a linked list (push at head)

problem.name: Code360 - Implement Stack With Linked List

files.what: A stack on a singly linked list where the **head** is the top: push and pop both happen at the head in O(1).
steps: `push`: new node points to the old `head`, then becomes `head`; `size++`.
`pop`: if not empty, move `head` forward, delete the old node, `size--`.
`getTop` returns `head->data`, or `-1` when empty.
The judge supplies `Node`; the harness prelude defines it.
files.complexity: Time O(1) per operation · Space O(n)
files.input:
9
push 4
push 8
top
size
pop
top
pop
isEmpty
top
files.input_note: Number of commands, then one per line (`push x`, `pop`, `top`, `size`, `isEmpty`).
files.output_note: Push 4, 8 → `top -> 8`, `size -> 2`; after one pop `top -> 4`; after another the stack is empty and `top -> -1`.

check.q: Why is the head a good top for a singly linked stack?
check.a: Adding and removing at the head needs no walk and no `prev` pointer, so both are O(1).

files.title: Queue with a linked list (first version)

problem.name: Code360 - Queue Using Array or Singly Linked List

files.what: Code360's queue class: `enqueue`, `dequeue` (returns the value or -1), `front`, `isEmpty`. This first version walks the whole list to add at the end.
steps: `enqueue`: if empty the node becomes `head`; otherwise walk `tmp` to the last node and link after it.
`dequeue`: return `-1` if empty; otherwise save `head->data`, move `head`, delete the old node.
`front` returns `head->data` or `-1`.

enqueue 10
enqueue 20
front
dequeue

check.a: It walks from `head` to the last node every time instead of using the `tail` pointer.

problem.name: Code360 - Queue Using Array or Singly Linked List

files.what: The fixed version: keeps a `tail` pointer so `enqueue` is O(1), and initialises `size = 0`.
steps: `enqueue`: empty → `head = tail = newNode`; otherwise `tail->next = newNode; tail = newNode`.
`dequeue`: move `head`; if it becomes `NULL`, also set `tail = NULL`.

files.title: Insert an element at the bottom of a stack

problem.name: Code360 - Insert An Element At Its Bottom In A Given Stack

files.what: Empties the stack into a helper stack, pushes `x`, then pours the helper back — so `x` ends up under everything.
steps: Pop all values of `st` into `new_st` (their order flips).
`st.push(x)` — `x` is now the only value, i.e. the bottom.
Pop `new_st` back into `st` (the order flips back to the original).
Harness prints the result from bottom to top, like the problem statement.
files.input_note: `T`, then for each case `N X` and `N` stack values listed bottom to top.
files.output_note: The statement's example: `[7, 1, 4, 5]` with `x = 9` gives `9 7 1 4 5`. The second case `[8]`, `x = 2` gives `2 8`.
files.watch_out: `int val;` is declared but never used — harmless.

check.q: How could you do this without a second stack?
check.a: With recursion: pop the top, recursively insert `x` at the bottom, then push the popped value back (the call stack is the helper).

files.title: Insert at the bottom of a stack (copy)

problem.name: Code360 - Insert An Element At Its Bottom In A Given Stack

files.what: Same function as the Code360 file above.
steps: Pour into a helper stack, push `x`, pour back.
files.input_note: `T`, then `N X` and `N` values bottom to top.
files.output_note: `[1, 2, 3]` with `x = 0` becomes `0 1 2 3` (bottom to top).

check.q: After the first pouring loop, which value is on top of `new_st`?
check.a: The old bottom value (`1` in this example).

files.title: Reverse a queue
files.what: Moves every value from the queue into a stack, then back into the queue — the stack flips the order.
steps: While `q` has values: push `q.front()` onto `st`, pop `q`.
While `st` has values: push `st.top()` into `q`, pop `st`.
Return `q`.
files.input_note: `T`, then for each case `N` and `N` values (front first).
files.output_note: The problem's Sample 1: `9` stays `9`; `10 6 8 12 3` becomes `3 12 8 6 10` — matches the expected output.

check.q: Why is `q` passed by value here?
check.a: The function works on its own copy and returns the reversed copy; the caller's queue is untouched.

files.title: Reverse a queue (copy)
files.what: Same solution as `code360_reverse_a_queue.cpp`.
steps: Queue → stack → queue.
files.input_note: `T`, then `N` and `N` values per case.
files.output_note: The problem's Sample 2: `99 89` → `89 99`, `1..6` → `6 5 4 3 2 1`, as expected.

check.q: What would happen if you moved the queue into another queue instead of a stack?
check.a: The order would stay the same — a queue keeps order, only a stack reverses it.

files.title: Reverse the first K elements of a queue

problem.name: Code360 - Reverse First K Elements of Queue

files.what: Reverses only the first `k` values and keeps the rest in order, using a stack and a rotation.
steps: If `k == 0` or `k > size`, return the queue unchanged.
Pop the first `k` values into a stack.
Push them back from the stack — they are now reversed but sit at the **back**.
Rotate the other `size - k` values: take each from the front and push it to the back.
Now the reversed block is at the front.
files.input_note: `T`, then for each case `N K` and `N` values.
files.output_note: `1 2 3 4 5` with `k = 3` → `3 2 1 4 5`. With `k = n = 4`, the whole queue is reversed: `40 30 20 10`.
files.watch_out: The rotation loop recomputes `q.size() - k` every round; it works only because each round pushes one and pops one, keeping the size fixed.

check.q: After step 3 for `1 2 3 4 5`, `k = 3`, what does the queue look like?
check.a: `4 5 3 2 1` — the reversed block is at the back until the rotation moves `4 5` behind it.

files.title: Maximum equal stack sum
files.what: Three stacks of positive numbers. Keep removing from the stack with the largest sum until all three sums are equal; that sum is the answer.
steps: `getSum` takes a copy of a stack and adds up its values.
Loop: if `sum1 == sum2 == sum3`, stop.
Otherwise pop from the stack whose sum is largest and subtract that value from its sum.
Return the common sum (0 if everything had to be removed).
files.complexity: Time O(n1 + n2 + n3) · Space O(n) for the sum copies
files.input_note: `T`, then per case three stacks, each as `N` followed by values from bottom to top (a simpler format than the judge's `-1`-terminated lines).
files.output_note: Case 1 is the statement's picture (sums 16, 23, 8) → `8`. Case 2 (`1`, `5`, `3`) can only be equal when all are empty → `0`.
files.watch_out: Values go up to 10^9 and a stack can hold 10^4 of them, so the sums can overflow `int`; `long long` sums are safer.

check.q: Why pop from the tallest (largest-sum) stack?
check.a: Sums only go down, so the smallest sum is an upper limit; only stacks above it need to shrink.

files.title: Maximum equal stack sum (copy)
files.what: Same code as `code360_maximum_equal_stack_sum.cpp`, with the problem statement in the comment.
steps: Pop from the largest-sum stack until all three sums match.
files.complexity: Time O(n1 + n2 + n3) · Space O(n)
files.input_note: `T`, then three stacks as `N` + values bottom to top.
files.output_note: Stacks `1 1 1`, `1 2`, `3` already have equal sums, so nothing is popped and the answer is `3`.

check.q: Can the loop run forever?
check.a: No. Each round removes one positive value; at worst all stacks become empty and the sums are all 0.

files.title: Delete node in a linked list (review)

problem.name: LeetCode 237 - Delete Node in a Linked List

files.what: Same trick as Module 11: copy the next node's value into this node and skip the next node.
steps: `node->val = node->next->val`.
`node->next = node->next->next`.
Harness: builds the list, finds the node with the target value, and calls `deleteNode`.
files.input_note: `n`, the `n` values, then the value of the node to delete.
files.output_note: LeetCode's example: `4 5 1 9`, delete `5` → `4 1 9`.

check.q: Can this function delete the last node?
check.a: No — there is no next node to copy from; the problem promises it won't be the tail.

files.title: Intersection of two linked lists (review)

problem.name: LeetCode 160 - Intersection of Two Linked Lists

files.what: Brute force from Module 11: for every node of A, scan all of B and compare addresses.
steps: Outer loop over A, inner loop over B.
Return the first node where `tempA == tempB`, else `NULL`.
Harness: builds the A-only part, the B-only part and a shared tail, and links them.
files.input_note: `T`; per case three lists (`n` + values): only-in-A, only-in-B, shared.
files.output_note: Case 1 is LeetCode's example (shared tail `8 4 5`) → intersect at `8`. Case 2 has no shared tail → `No intersection`.

check.q: What does the harness do to make the two lists really share nodes?
check.a: It points the last node of each list at the same `common` list, so the tail nodes are the same objects in memory.

files.title: Linked list cycle (review)
files.what: Floyd's fast/slow pointers, as in Module 11.
steps: `slow` moves 1 step, `fast` 2 steps.
Meeting means a cycle; `fast` reaching `NULL` means none.
Harness: `pos` says which node the tail links back to (`-1` = no link), like LeetCode.
files.input_note: `T`; per case `n`, the values, then `pos`.
files.output_note: `3 2 0 4` with `pos 1` → `true`; `1..5` with `pos -1` → `false`; a single node linked to itself → `true`.

check.q: Does a single node pointing to itself count as a cycle here?
check.a: Yes: after one round `slow` and `fast` are both that node, so they meet.

files.title: Merge nodes in between zeros

problem.name: LeetCode 2181 - Merge Nodes in Between Zeros

files.what: The list starts and ends with `0`. Each run of numbers between two zeros is replaced by one node holding their sum, re-using the existing nodes.
steps: `modify` is the node that will store the next sum (starts at `head->next`); `nextSum` scans ahead.
Add values into `sum` until `nextSum` reaches a `0`.
Store `sum` in `modify->val`, step `nextSum` past the zero, and link `modify->next = nextSum`.
Move `modify` to that node and repeat until `nextSum` is `NULL`.
Return `head->next` (skipping the first zero).
files.input_note: `T`; per case `n` and the list values.
files.watch_out: On the last round `nextSum` becomes `NULL`, so `modify` becomes `NULL` too — fine, because the loop then stops before `modify` is used again.

check.q: Why does the answer start at `head->next`?
check.a: The first node is always the leading `0`, which is not part of any sum.

files.title: Palindrome linked list (review)
files.what: Module 11's approach: copy the list, reverse the copy recursively, compare the two.
steps: Copy with `insert_at_tail`.
`reverse(newHead, newHead)`.
Walk both lists together; any mismatch → `false`.
files.input_note: `T`; per case `n` and the values.
files.output_note: `1 2 2 1` → `true` (LeetCode's example), `1 2` → `false`, `1 2 3 2 1` → `true`.

check.q: What extra memory does this solution use?
check.a: A full copy of the list (O(n)), plus O(n) recursion depth for the reverse.

files.title: Remove duplicates from sorted list (review)

problem.name: LeetCode 83 - Remove Duplicates from Sorted List

files.what: Same as Module 11: skip the next node while it has the same value.
steps: If `temp->val == temp->next->val`, unlink `temp->next`; otherwise advance `temp`.
files.input_note: `T`; per case `n` and the sorted values.
files.output_note: `1 1 2 3 3` → `1 2 3`; `7 7 7 7` → `7` (shows why `temp` must not move after a removal).

check.q: For `7 7 7 7`, how many times does `temp` move forward?
check.a: Zero — every comparison finds a duplicate and removes it, until `temp->next` is `NULL`.

files.title: Remove N-th node from end of list

problem.name: LeetCode 19 - Remove Nth Node From End of List

files.what: Counts the length, turns 'n-th from the end' into an index from the front, and unlinks that node.
steps: Count nodes into `length`.
If `n == length`, the head is the target: move `head` forward and delete the old head.
Otherwise walk `tmp` to the node **before** the target (index `length - n - 1`).
Unlink and delete `tmp->next`.
files.input_note: `T`; per case `n` values as a list, then the `n` to remove.
files.output_note: `1 2 3 4 5`, `n = 2` → `1 2 3 5` (LeetCode's example). A one-node list with `n = 1` becomes empty. `1 2` with `n = 2` removes the head → `2`.

check.q: Why is removing the head a special case?
check.a: There is no node before the head whose `next` could be changed; the head pointer itself must move.

files.title: Reverse linked list (review)
files.what: Module 11's recursive reverse, submitted as a pure solution.
steps: Recurse to the last node and make it `head`.
On return: `tmp->next->next = tmp; tmp->next = NULL;`.
An empty list is returned as-is.
files.input_note: `T`; per case `n` and the values (`0` = empty list).
files.output_note: `1 2 3 4 5` → `5 4 3 2 1`; the empty list stays empty (the `head == NULL` guard).

check.q: What would happen without the `head == NULL` check?
check.a: `reverse` would read `tmp->next` on a `NULL` pointer and crash.

files.title: Swapping nodes in a linked list (review)

problem.name: LeetCode 1721 - Swapping Nodes in a Linked List

files.what: Module 11's solution: find the k-th node from each end by counting, then swap their values.
steps: Count `length`.
`frontNode` = k-th from start (`k-1` steps).
`endNode` = k-th from end (`length-k` steps).
`swap` the two values.
files.input_note: `T`; per case the list (`n` + values), then `k`.

check.q: What happens when `k` points to the same node from both ends (e.g. middle of an odd list)?
check.a: The node is swapped with itself, so nothing changes.

Reverse First K Elements of Queue
Insert An Element At Its Bottom In A Given Stack

recap: Queue = FIFO: push at the back, pop at the front, both O(1).
On a singly linked list: add at `tail`, remove at `head`, and reset `tail` when the queue empties.
Stack in the middle reverses order; queue in the middle keeps it.
Brackets, backspaces, adjacent pairs → think stack.
Min stack: a second stack of minimums, pushed on `<=`.
Moving a stack into another stack twice gives back the original order.

check_yourself.q: You push 1, 2, 3 into a queue and pop once. What are `front()` and `back()`?
How would you check whether a queue's values read the same forwards and backwards using STL containers?
check_yourself.a: Copy the values into a stack as well; then pop the queue and the stack together and compare — the stack gives the reverse order.

check_yourself.q: In 'queue using stacks', which operation becomes expensive and why?
check_yourself.a: `pop`/`peek`: the oldest value is at the bottom of the stack, so everything above it must be moved to reach it.

check_yourself.q: Why does the Code360 queue need `tail = NULL` when the last element is dequeued?
check_yourself.a: Otherwise `tail` is a dangling pointer to freed memory, and the next `enqueue` would link a node through it.

body: Stand in a line at a ticket counter. You arrive and join at the back. The person being served is at the front, and when they are done they leave and everyone shifts up one. Nobody who arrived after you is served before you.
That is a **queue**: first in, first out — **FIFO**. It is the opposite habit to the pile of plates in Module 13. A stack hands back the newest value; a queue hands back the oldest one.
intro.trace:
front                                 back
  v                                     v
[ 10 ] [ 20 ] [ 30 ]   <- new joins here
  ^
served and removed here

body: A queue has two ends that matter, so it has six small operations: `push` (join at the back), `pop` (leave from the front), `front` and `back` to read the two ends, plus `size` and `empty`. As with the stack, every one of them is O(1).
Follow a short line with real values. Watch how `front` and `back` move independently of each other. With the STL that whole trace is five lines of code.
intro.trace:
push 10    [ 10 ]          front 10  back 10
push 20    [ 10 20 ]       front 10  back 20
push 30    [ 10 20 30 ]    front 10  back 30
pop        [ 20 30 ]       front 20  back 30
push 40    [ 20 30 40 ]    front 20  back 40
pop        [ 30 40 ]       front 30  back 40

body: **Which end goes where.** Building a queue on a singly linked list is the part that catches people. Add at the `tail` and remove at the `head`, and both are O(1). Do it the other way round and `pop` would have to find the node *before* the tail, which means walking the whole list — O(n) for every value removed. The choice of ends is not a matter of taste; one of them is 100000 times slower on a long queue.

There is one more detail the module keeps coming back to. When the last value leaves, `head` becomes `NULL`, and `tail` must be set to `NULL` as well. Forget it and `tail` still points at memory you have just freed, so the next `push` links a new node onto a deleted node.

The module also builds the queue on a doubly linked list and on the STL `list` — `push_back` to join, `pop_front` to leave — before using the ready-made `queue<int>`. Same six operations every time, different storage underneath.
**Why have both a stack and a queue?** Because of one difference, and the practice problems on this page are mostly that difference in disguise. Put the same values into each, then take them all out:
intro.trace:
put in       10  20  30  40  50
stack gives  50  40  30  20  10   (reversed)
queue gives  10  20  30  40  50   (same order)

body: So a stack in the middle of a pipeline **reverses**, and a queue **keeps the order**. That is the whole method behind reversing a queue: pour it into a stack, then pour the stack back. Reversing only the first `k` values is the same trick applied to a prefix, followed by rotating the rest round to the back.

**When you want a stack.** Whenever the thing to deal with next is the most recent one still unresolved: matching brackets, applying backspaces to typed text, cancelling adjacent equal letters. **When you want a queue.** Whenever fairness of arrival matters, or work must be processed in the order it was created.

The rest of the page is practice. There are the four practice-day problems, then LeetCode and Code360 classics: valid parentheses, min stack (a second stack holding only the minimums, so `getMin` stays O(1)), a stack built out of queues and a queue built out of stacks, insert at the bottom of a stack, and maximum equal stack sum. The last group revisits Module 11's linked list problems. Files that were written straight into a judge hold only a class or a function, so the page adds a small test driver to let them run.
